title: Whisky Explained
description: A self-paced introduction to whisky as a craft with a long history, from medieval monks to its place worldwide today. Each module has a short lesson, expert insights and a quiz. For bartenders, retailers and whisky enthusiasts.
topics: History: from medieval monks to global prominence
Production: from grain selection to barrel ageing
Styles: single malt, blended, Scotch, bourbon, Australian whisky and more
Rules and regulations around the world
How to drink it: nosing, tasting and serving

lessons.title: Welcome to Whisky Explained
lessons.review:
Whisky is a spirit distilled from a fermented mash of grain, then aged in wooden casks. Barley, corn, rye and wheat are the usual grains, and the wood is almost always oak.

You will see two spellings. Whisky is used in Scotland, Canada, Japan and Australia; whiskey is used in Ireland and most of the United States. Same family, different traditions.

This course walks from history to production, the categories of Scotch, the rules that protect them, and how to taste like a pro.

lessons.title: The history of Scotch whisky
lessons.review:
The Gaelic uisge beatha, "water of life", gave us the word whisky. Distilling is thought to have reached Scotland with monks, and the first written record comes from the Exchequer Rolls of 1494: malt sent to Friar John Cor "wherewith to make aquavitae".

For centuries much of Scotland's whisky was made illegally to avoid tax. The Excise Act of 1823 made licensed distilling worthwhile, and many famous distilleries date from that era.

The column still, patented by Aeneas Coffey in 1830, made light grain whisky quick to produce. Blending it with malt created the smooth blended Scotch that conquered the world, helped when phylloxera devastated Europe's vineyards and brandy ran short in the late 1800s.

questions.explain: Uisge beatha is Gaelic for "water of life".

lessons.title: How whisky is produced
lessons.review:
Malting: barley is soaked, allowed to germinate so its starches can become sugars, then dried in a kiln. Burning peat in the kiln gives smoky, peated whisky.

Mashing and fermenting: the ground malt is mixed with hot water to release sugary wort. Yeast turns it into a beer-like wash of around 7–9% ABV.

Distilling and maturing: malt whisky is usually distilled twice in copper pot stills; grain whisky is made in column stills. The new spirit then matures in oak casks, where a little evaporates each year: the "angels' share".

questions.explain: Peat burnt in the kiln flavours the malt.

lessons.title: The categories of Scotch whisky
lessons.review:
Scotch has five legal categories. Single Malt: 100% malted barley, distilled in pot stills at one distillery. Single Grain: made at one distillery, which can use other cereals.

Blended Malt mixes single malts from several distilleries. Blended Grain mixes single grains. Blended Scotch Whisky combines malt and grain whiskies and is the biggest seller of all.

"Single" means one distillery, not one cask. Knowing the category tells your customer a lot about the style before they taste.

questions.q: How many legal categories of Scotch are there?
questions.explain: Single Malt, Single Grain, Blended Malt, Blended Grain and Blended Scotch.

questions.q: What does "single" mean in Single Malt?
questions.explain: Single refers to one distillery.
Blends make up most Scotch sold worldwide.

lessons.title: Rules and regulations of Scotch
lessons.review:
Scotch is protected by law (the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009). It must be distilled and matured in Scotland, in oak casks, for at least three years.

It must be bottled at no less than 40% ABV, and nothing may be added except water and plain caramel colouring.

An age statement on the label always refers to the youngest whisky in the bottle. A 12-year-old blend can contain much older whisky, but nothing younger than 12.

questions.explain: At least three years in oak casks in Scotland.
Scotch must be bottled at 40% ABV or more.

questions.explain: Age statements always state the youngest component.

lessons.title: How to drink whisky like a pro
lessons.review:
Start with the right glass: a tulip-shaped glass such as a Glencairn gathers the aromas. Look at the colour and the "legs" running down the glass.

Nose gently with your mouth slightly open, then taste: let the whisky coat your palate, and notice the finish after you swallow.

A few drops of water can open up aromas, especially in stronger whiskies. Neat, on the rocks or in a highball are all correct; the best way is the one the drinker enjoys.

questions.explain: The shape gathers aromas toward the nose.

questions.q: What can a few drops of water do?
questions.explain: Water can release aromatic compounds.

options: The last drop in the bottle
questions.explain: Finish is how the flavour lingers.

lessons.title: Whisky summary
lessons.review:
Whisky is fermented grain, distilled and aged in oak. Scotland gave us the name and the rules, and the Coffey still gave us blends.

Malting, mashing, fermenting, distilling and maturing shape every bottle. Scotch has five categories, a three-year minimum and a 40% ABV minimum.

Taste with a good glass, look, nose, taste and finish, and recommend whisky the way your customer likes to drink it.
